```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
library(lattice)
b <- readRDS("parallel-benchmark.rds")

# median time over the replications
tm <- aggregate(time ~ scenario + approach + workers + m, b$timings, median)
# short labels for the panels
panel_labels <- c(
  small = "Small data (pmm)",
  large = "Large data (pmm)",
  slow = "Slow method (rf)"
)
tm$scenario <- factor(tm$scenario, names(b$scenarios), b$scenarios)
tm$panel <- factor(
  panel_labels[names(b$scenarios)[as.integer(tm$scenario)]],
  panel_labels
)
# earlier runs stored the label "mice(parallel = TRUE)"
tm$approach[tm$approach == "mice(parallel = TRUE)"] <- "mice(future = TRUE)"
tm$approach <- factor(
  tm$approach,
  c("mice()", "mice(future = TRUE)", "futuremice()")
)
get <- function(s, a, w, m) {
  tm$time[tm$scenario == b$scenarios[[s]] & tm$approach == a &
    tm$workers == w & tm$m == m]
}
seq_time <- function(s, m) get(s, "mice()", 1, m)
par_time <- function(s, w, m) get(s, "mice(future = TRUE)", w, m)
fut_time <- function(s, w, m) get(s, "futuremice()", w, m)
f1 <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
f2 <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)

startup <- aggregate(cbind(cold, warm) ~ workers, b$startup, median)
startup$cost <- startup$cold - startup$warm
```

## Introduction

This vignette measures when running the chains in parallel pays off,
and compares `mice(future = TRUE)` with sequential `mice()` and with
the wrapper `futuremice()` [@volker-2022-1]. It follows the design of
@volker-2022-1, and adds a slow imputation method and more numbers of
imputations. The vignette [Parallel imputation](parallel.html) explains
how to use `future = TRUE`.

The timings were computed beforehand with the script
`data-raw/parallel-benchmark.R` in the source of the package, and are
read from a file. They depend on the machine, so treat them as an
indication of the pattern, not as absolute numbers. The results below
were obtained on:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
info <- b$info
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Item = c("Date", "CPU", "Cores", "R", "mice", "future"),
  Value = c(
    format(info$date), info$cpu, info$cores, info$R, info$mice,
    info$future
  )
))
```

## Design

The data are drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with zero
means, unit variances and correlations of 0.5. Eighty percent of the
cases get missing values, completely at random (MCAR), by `ampute()`.
There are three scenarios:

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = names(b$scenarios),
  Description = unname(b$scenarios)
))
```

The `rf` method fits a random forest with the `ranger` package for every
variable in every iteration, which makes it much slower than `pmm`.
`ranger` uses two threads by default, also within a worker. All
runs use `maxit = `r b$maxit``, and every combination is repeated
`r b$reps` times; the figures show the median time. We compare:

* **`mice()`**: the sequential sampler, on one core.
* **`mice(future = TRUE)`**: the parallel sampler, on a `multisession`
  plan with 2, 4 or 8 workers that was started before the timing, so that
  the workers are reused. This is how you would use it for repeated
  imputations (see below for the cost of starting workers).
* **`futuremice()`**: the wrapper with `n.core` set to 2, 4 or 8. It
  starts and closes its own workers in every call, so these timings
  include the start-up of the workers.

## Starting the workers

Each worker is a separate R session. A new worker has to start R and
load `mice` and its dependencies before it can impute. The table shows
the median time of a tiny imputation on new workers (cold) and on
workers that are already running (warm):

```{r, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Workers = startup$workers,
    `Cold (s)` = f2(startup$cold),
    `Warm (s)` = f2(startup$warm),
    `Start-up (s)` = f2(startup$cost),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "r"
)
```

Starting the workers costs about `r f1(mean(startup$cost))` seconds per
call on this machine. `futuremice()` pays this cost in every call.
`mice(future = TRUE)` uses the workers of the plan set by the user, so
with `future::plan(multisession, workers = 4)` it pays the cost only for
the first call. For a single long imputation the difference does not matter, but
for many short imputations, for example in a simulation study, it does.

## Results

```{r timings, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Median time (seconds) against the number of imputations m, per scenario and number of workers. Note the different vertical scales."}
tm$series <- ifelse(
  tm$approach == "mice()",
  "mice()",
  paste0(tm$approach, ", ", tm$workers, " workers")
)
lev <- c(
  "mice()",
  paste0("mice(future = TRUE), ", c(2, 4, 8), " workers"),
  paste0("futuremice(), ", c(2, 4, 8), " workers")
)
tm$series <- factor(tm$series, lev)
cols <- c("black", "#9ecae1", "#4292c6", "#08519c", "#fdae6b", "#f16913", "#a63603")
xyplot(
  time ~ m | panel,
  data = tm,
  groups = series,
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  cex = 0.6,
  col = cols,
  layout = c(3, 1),
  scales = list(
    y = list(relation = "free"),
    x = list(at = c(5, 20, 50, 100), alternating = FALSE)
  ),
  xlab = "Number of imputations m",
  ylab = "Time (seconds)",
  key = list(
    space = "bottom",
    columns = 2,
    lines = list(col = cols, lwd = 2),
    text = list(lev, cex = 0.8)
  )
)
```

```{r speedup, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Speed-up of mice(future = TRUE) relative to sequential mice(), for m = 100. The dashed line is the ideal speed-up, equal to the number of workers."}
sp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(b$scenarios), function(s) {
  data.frame(
    scenario = panel_labels[[s]],
    workers = c(2, 4, 8),
    speedup = seq_time(s, 100) / sapply(c(2, 4, 8), par_time, s = s, m = 100)
  )
}))
xyplot(
  speedup ~ workers,
  data = sp,
  groups = factor(scenario, panel_labels),
  type = "b",
  pch = 19,
  col = c("#2ca25f", "#3182bd", "#e6550d"),
  key = list(
    space = "right",
    lines = list(col = c("#2ca25f", "#3182bd", "#e6550d"), lwd = 2),
    text = list(unname(panel_labels))
  ),
  panel = function(...) {
    panel.abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
    panel.xyplot(...)
  },
  scales = list(x = list(at = c(2, 4, 8))),
  xlab = "Number of workers",
  ylab = "Speed-up"
)
```

### When does it pay off?

* **Small data.** For 1000 cases and 4 variables, one imputation takes
  a few milliseconds. Sequential `mice()` needs
  `r f2(seq_time("small", 5))` seconds for `m = 5` and
  `r f2(seq_time("small", 100))` seconds for `m = 100`. On running
  workers, `mice(future = TRUE)` with 8 workers needs
  `r f2(par_time("small", 8, 100))` seconds for `m = 100`. But if the
  workers have to be started first, the start-up cost of about
  `r f1(mean(startup$cost))` seconds is larger than the whole sequential
  run for small `m`. For small data, parallel imputation only helps with
  many imputations, on workers that are already running.

* **Large data.** For 10000 cases and 8 variables, `mice()` takes
  `r f1(seq_time("large", 5))` seconds for `m = 5` and
  `r f1(seq_time("large", 100))` seconds for `m = 100`. With 8 workers,
  this becomes `r f2(par_time("large", 8, 5))` and
  `r f1(par_time("large", 8, 100))` seconds, a speed-up of
  `r f1(seq_time("large", 100) / par_time("large", 8, 100))` for
  `m = 100`. Including the start-up of new workers, parallel imputation
  pays off from `m = 20` on; for `m = 5` the gain is small.

* **Slow method.** With `rf`, `mice()` takes
  `r f1(seq_time("slow", 100))` seconds for `m = 100`, and
  `mice(future = TRUE)` with 8 workers
  `r f1(par_time("slow", 8, 100))` seconds, a speed-up of
  `r f1(seq_time("slow", 100) / par_time("slow", 8, 100))`. The slower
  the imputation, the smaller the share of the fixed costs, and the closer
  the speed-up gets to the number of workers.

* **Number of workers.** The speed-up grows with the number of workers,
  but less than proportionally (second figure). With `m` chains, at most
  `m` workers can be busy, and with `m = 5` and 8 workers, three workers
  are idle. Each worker also has to receive the data and return its
  chains.

The time per chain is the same for all values of `m`, so a parallel run
takes roughly the time of `m / workers` sequential chains, plus a fixed
overhead. A rule of thumb: if one sequential run takes less than a few
seconds, the parallel run saves little; if it takes minutes, the parallel
run is close to `workers` times faster.

### Comparison with `futuremice()`

`futuremice()` splits the `m` imputations into one block per worker,
and runs a complete `mice()` call for each block, including its own
set-up and starting imputations. The blocks are then combined with
`ibind()`. `mice(future = TRUE)` sets up the imputation model and the
starting imputations once, and only runs the chains on the workers.

For `m = 100` with 8 workers, `futuremice()` took
`r f1(fut_time("large", 8, 100))` seconds for the large data and
`r f1(fut_time("slow", 8, 100))` seconds for the slow method, against
`r f1(par_time("large", 8, 100))` and `r f1(par_time("slow", 8, 100))`
seconds for `mice(future = TRUE)`. About
`r f1(mean(startup$cost))` seconds of the difference is the start-up of
the workers, which `futuremice()` pays in every call. The remainder is
probably due to the repeated set-up per block and the combining of the
blocks. For small data, the start-up cost dominates: `futuremice()` is
only faster than sequential `mice()` for `m = 100`
(`r f2(fut_time("small", 8, 100))` against
`r f2(seq_time("small", 100))` seconds with 8 workers).

## Moving from `futuremice()` to `mice(future = TRUE)`

Most arguments of `futuremice()` have a direct counterpart, or are no
longer needed:

| `futuremice()` | `mice(future = TRUE)` |
|:---------------|:------------------------|
| `n.core = 4` | set up the workers once with `future::plan(multisession, workers = 4)` |
| `parallelseed = 123` | `seed = 123` |
| `seed` (gives identical imputations on all cores) | not needed |
| `use.logical = FALSE` | `future::plan(multisession, workers = parallelly::availableCores(logical = FALSE))` |
| `future.plan = "multicore"` | `future::plan(multicore)` before the call |
| `packages = "miceadds"` | not needed: methods from packages are loaded on the workers, if installed |
| `globals = "mice.impute.mymethod"` | not needed: user-written methods, their helper functions and objects used in `post` are sent along |
| `...` | `...` |

The results differ in a few other ways:

* **Reproducibility.** `futuremice()` gives reproducible results for a
  given `parallelseed` and `n.core`. `mice(future = TRUE)` gives the
  same imputations for a given `seed`, whatever the number of workers.
* **Plan.** `futuremice()` sets up its own plan in every call, and
  restores the previous plan when it returns. `mice(future = TRUE)` never
  sets up or changes a plan: it uses the plan set by the user.
* **Logged events.** `ibind()` keeps the `loggedEvents` of the first
  block only, so `futuremice()` drops the events logged by the other
  workers. `mice(future = TRUE)` collects the events of all chains.
* **Continuing.** An object from `mice(future = TRUE)` can be continued
  with `mice.mids()`, in parallel, with the same result as a single run.
* **Starting imputations.** `futuremice()` draws the starting imputations
  separately for each block; `mice(future = TRUE)` draws them once, as
  `mice()` does.

## Reproducing the benchmark

To rerun the benchmark on your own machine, install the version of
`mice` to test (the workers load the installed version), and run from
the root of the source package:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
source("data-raw/parallel-benchmark.R")
```

This takes about half an hour on a laptop, and writes
`vignettes/parallel-benchmark.rds`.
